front.title: The Sample Files
body: Every practice page in this book uses the same small set of files: two years of sales from one bike shop, made up for this series. Nothing in them is real, and they come with the book.

Start from **Sales clean.xlsx** loaded, with Sales related to Products on Product and to Customers on CustomerID. That's where book one left off. If you haven't got that file open, load the three sheets and drag those two columns across in Model view. It takes a minute.

The model is the one every page in this book draws: a Sales table with Amount, Qty, Price and OrderDate, a Products table with Category, a Customers table, and from the time intelligence part on, a Date table you'll build yourself.
The answers to every practice page are at the back.

back.title: Answers
body: ## Practice: Which Kind
116,922 in both cards. The measure works it out when the card asks; the column worked it out once per row at load and stored it.
Power BI can't tell which table Amount belongs to, so the formula turns red. With the table name in front, it always can.
Still 116,922. Line breaks are for you, not for the engine.
## Practice: Context
Card 116,922; Cycles 80,680, Gear 28,809, blank 7,433. The blank row is the lamp, which has no row on the Products sheet and so no category.
116,922 on every row. The row context tells the column which row it's on; it doesn't narrow what SUM sees.
80,680 everywhere. Blue is only the bike, and CALCULATE's filter on Colour applies in every cell, whatever the row's category was asking.
## Practice: Functions
99.42, 6 and 840. The smallest line is one bell; the largest is two bikes at full price.
1,176 against 1,179. COUNT skips the 3 blank amounts; COUNTROWS counts every row regardless. DISTINCTCOUNT of Product is 5.
61.83 overall, and 6 for the bell. Dividing total amount by total quantity gives a real average unit price, and a product with one price ever gives that price back exactly.
## Practice: Iterators
116,922 with SUMX, about 139,358 the other way. Multiplying a total quantity by an average price assumes every unit sold at the average, and bikes didn't.
5,846.10. AVERAGEX walked the Customers table, worked out Total Sales for each one, and averaged those twenty answers.
207 blank rows, all lamps. There's no lamp on the Products sheet, so there's no related row and RELATED hands back nothing.
## Practice: Filters
116,922 in every row. ALL(Sales) strips the category filter the row put on, so the measure sees the whole table while the visual stays sliced.
69.0%. Bikes are most of the money. The top of the fraction keeps the row's filter; the bottom removes it.
West, then All regions, then All regions. SELECTEDVALUE only hands back a value when the column is down to exactly one.
## Practice: Dates
731 rows: every day of 2024 and 2025, both whole years. Marking it lets Power BI check for gaps and drop the hidden date tables it was making for you.
4,388 for June alone, 28,131 from January to the end of June. TOTALYTD changed the date filter to run from the start of the year, then evaluated.
3,877, and the difference is 511. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifted the selected June back a year and handed those dates to CALCULATE.
## Practice: Craft
69.0%, unchanged. The variables didn't change the maths; they named the two halves so the next person, probably you, can read it.
The formatted version puts DIVIDE, CALCULATE and ALL on their own lines with the brackets lined up. If it looks longer, that's the point: longer and readable beats short and opaque.
A table with a calculator icon at the top of the Data pane, holding nothing but measures. That's the file someone else can maintain.

publishing.description:
You can build a Power BI report without writing much DAX. You just can't build a good one.

Power BI DAX for Absolute Beginners picks up where the first book left off. Your data is in, there's a chart on the canvas, and now every real question you want to ask needs a formula. This is 28 short lessons, one idea per page, each with a clear diagram of what's actually happening and one small thing to try in the file you already have open.

Inside, you'll learn how to:
- Tell DAX apart from Excel formulas and from Power Query, and know which one you need
- Choose between a measure, a calculated column and a calculated table, and know why it matters
- Understand filter context and row context, the two ideas everything else rests on
- Use CALCULATE to change the question a measure is answering
- Count things without getting it quietly wrong, and divide without breaking the report
- Write iterators like SUMX, and know when you actually need the X
- Build a proper date table and compare this year to last year in one line
- Use VAR to write formulas you can still read in six months
- Avoid the handful of DAX mistakes almost every beginner makes

No unexplained acronyms, no assumed expertise, no wall of reference documentation. Every function turns up at the moment you need it, in the order you'll meet it.

By the last page, you won't be copying formulas off the internet and hoping. You'll know what they do.
publishing.audience: Readers who can already build a basic Power BI report and are ready to write real formulas.
